title: AI thermal cameras on a Madukkarai rail stretch in Tamil Nadu alert crews, who slow or stop trains for elephants; a train kills an elephant and her calf near Puthuppathi in August 2026
summary: The Tamil Nadu Forest Department's AI thermal cameras at Madukkarai sent over 7,116 alerts by 7 July 2026, with no elephant deaths there; a train killed two elephants nearby on 13 August 2026.
account: Eleven elephants were killed on the railway tracks of the Madukkarai stretch between 2008 and 2022, the last three in November 2021. Down To Earth reported that the Madras High Court had directed action on elephant deaths on the tracks in 2021. The Tamil Nadu Forest Department installed 24 hybrid thermal cameras with AI detection on 12 towers. They cover 7.05 km of the Ettimadai–Walayar railway section in Madukkarai forest range, Coimbatore district. A trial run had already generated alerts by 7 January 2024. The system has operated since 9 February 2024. Alerts go to a control room at Puthupathi. Its staff warn station masters and loco pilots and drive elephants away from the tracks. Down To Earth reported on 9 March 2025 that the Tamil Nadu government allocated 7.24 crore rupees for the system. On 21 December 2025 The New Indian Express reported no elephant deaths on the railway tracks of the stretch in the previous 22 months. By 7 July 2026 the department's Additional Chief Secretary reported over 7,116 alerts and 3,281 train slow-downs or stops (DT Next reports 3,821). The same statement gave about 9,481 safe elephant crossings and no elephant deaths on the stretch. The department had also added AI-powered drones to extend surveillance beyond the fixed cameras. On 13 August 2026 a train killed a mother elephant and her calf near Chavadippara Puthuppathi, and The New Indian Express placed the collision on the Tamil Nadu side of the border. The Times of India reported that no warning reached the loco pilot. A legal notice reported by The Hindu on 31 August 2026 places this collision and a February 2026 death on the Walayar-Kanjikode corridor, where the Kerala detection system was still in testing.
purpose: Detect elephants near railway tracks with thermal cameras and AI, alert forest staff and railway crews, and prevent train-elephant collisions.
system: AI-based elephant early warning system (24 hybrid thermal cameras on 12 towers, Elephant Control and Command Center, Puthupathi)
deployer: Tamil Nadu Forest Department (Department of Environment, Climate Change and Forests), with railway station masters at Walayar and Ettimadai and loco pilots
taxonomy_note: The collisions avoided are between trains and elephants, so the gain is shared with conservation.

ratings.reason: The reports count train stops and crossings, and no source counts injuries avoided by crews or passengers.

The department reports about 9,481 safe crossings and no track deaths for wild elephants as of July 2026 on a stretch that recorded eleven deaths from 2008 to 2022. The number of deaths that would otherwise have occurred remains unknown. A train killed two elephants near Puthuppathi on 13 August 2026.

ai_role.statement: AI classification of thermal-camera feeds generated the alerts that triggered staff intervention and train slow-downs. The figures (alerts, stops, crossings, zero deaths) are the department's own statements as reproduced verbatim in news reports. No official document is among the sources. No per-event counterfactual is established.

Replaced “Southern Railway” in deployer with the sources' station masters at Walayar and Ettimadai and loco pilots, restated the trial as already generating alerts by 7 January 2024 rather than beginning then, attributed the zero-deaths figure to the Forest Department alone and dropped “endangered” from the societal reason, because no cited source names Southern Railway, dates the trial's start, quotes the railway on deaths or calls the elephants endangered.
Benefit type set to Increased Product Safety under Trustible's full taxonomy of 23 types; it was Improved Environmental Sustainability among the six first used.
Added what the benefit is measured against and what happened later, from the cited sources.
Country of the deployer added from the organization's own site or a registry.
Rewrote a rating reason, the account and the statement of the system's part in shorter sentences, with abbreviations expanded; facts, figures and quotations unchanged.
Reworded the notes about which sources could be read; facts, figures and quotations unchanged.

Removed the link to AI Incident Database incident 219, whose poaching cameras watch for intruders. Incident 1678, in which a self-driving car struck a duck, was also left unlinked, because its general driving system differs from fixed trackside thermal cameras that warn train crews about elephants. No incident involves an animal-detection warning system for railways or roads.
Added four sources, four of them independent; dated the case to 9 February 2024 (observed); recorded one other attempt to repeat the benefit.
Edited the title, headline, summary, metric, account of events for accuracy and clarity; revised the depth ratings; restated earlier revision notes.

display.answer: The counts of alerts and crossings come from the Forest Department, mostly through statements by its Additional Chief Secretary that news reports reproduce. No official document or log is among the sources. The New Indian Express and The Times of India reported the collision of 13 August 2026. The Hindu reported a legal notice that followed it.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: The Tamil Nadu Forest Department's AI thermal cameras at Madukkarai sent over 7,116 alerts by 7 July 2026, with no elephant deaths there; a train killed two elephants nearby on 13 August 2026.
fields.account: Eleven elephants were killed on the railway tracks of the Madukkarai stretch between 2008 and 2022, the last three in November 2021. Down To Earth reported that the Madras High Court had directed action on elephant deaths on the tracks in 2021. The Tamil Nadu Forest Department installed 24 hybrid thermal cameras with AI detection on 12 towers. They cover 7.05 km of the Ettimadai–Walayar railway section in Madukkarai forest range, Coimbatore district. A trial run had already generated alerts by 7 January 2024. The system has operated since 9 February 2024. Alerts go to a control room at Puthupathi. Its staff warn station masters and loco pilots and drive elephants away from the tracks. Down To Earth reported on 9 March 2025 that the Tamil Nadu government allocated 7.24 crore rupees for the system. On 21 December 2025 The New Indian Express reported no elephant deaths on the railway tracks of the stretch in the previous 22 months. By 7 July 2026 the department's Additional Chief Secretary reported over 7,116 alerts and 3,281 train slow-downs or stops (DT Next reports 3,821). The same statement gave about 9,481 safe elephant crossings and no elephant deaths on the stretch. The department had also added AI-powered drones to extend surveillance beyond the fixed cameras. On 13 August 2026 a train killed a mother elephant and her calf near Chavadippara Puthuppathi, and The New Indian Express placed the collision on the Tamil Nadu side of the border. The Times of India reported that no warning reached the loco pilot. A legal notice reported by The Hindu on 31 August 2026 places this collision and a February 2026 death on the Walayar-Kanjikode corridor, where the Kerala detection system was still in testing.
